note: The city's high point. A single big dome — its rings are wide and even, so the slope is long and walkable.
Cloud forest under the tower. Rings bunch tight on the west face — that side is genuinely steep.
Noe Peak. The southern of the pair; the saddle between the two is the classic figure-eight.
Eureka Peak. Two summits, one contour ring wrapping both at the base — a textbook saddle.
West shoulder of the Twin Peaks massif, not a separate mountain.
A small steep knob — few rings, packed close together.
Chert outcrop. The tight ring cluster here is why the streets switchback.
A dune-sand hill standing alone west of the massif — its own closed ring set.
A spur off Twin Peaks: its rings never close separately, they hang off the big massif.
Geographic centre of the city, marked by an empty pedestal.
The oldest park in the city, and a cleanly isolated cone on the map.
A long ridge, not a peak — rings run as stretched ovals, not circles.
Bare red chert. Contours crowd on the quarried east face.
An island of high ground in the flat southeast — surrounded by wide, empty low country.
Southwest corner high point, part of the old Merced dune belt.
Once a cemetery hill; the terraced west steps are visible as bunched rings.
A grassy whaleback. Long axis runs east–west — the rings are ovals.
An island inside Stow Lake — a hill entirely ringed by water.
Cable-car hill. Modest height, brutal grade — the rings are close together.
A ridge along the north shore, dropping hard to the Marina flats.
Western continuation of the same north-shore ridge line.
A tiny outlier between Noe Valley and Glen Canyon.
The eastern ridge — steep on the north face, easy on the south.
Home of Lombard Street's switchbacks: eight turns to cross four contour lines.
Quarried away on its east side — contours nearly touch there. That is a cliff.
A perfect little cone, ringed by one circular street.
A low reservoir mound in the southeast.
A gentle rise above the old Laurel Hill cemetery grounds.
The newest named hill on the list — added to the roster in the 1960s.
The far northwest clifftop, standing over the Pacific.
Cut in half for the Bay Bridge approach. Barely a bump on the map now.
